meta.title: How authentication works
meta.subtitle: Where identity is established, what is trusted downstream, and the two things that bypass it

sections.title: Where identity is established
sections.narrative:
Authentication happens in exactly one place. The BFF issues an opaque session token and keeps the user id against it server-side [[session.issued-by-bff]]; the token itself carries no claims, so there is nothing in it to forge or decode.

A session lasts twelve hours from the moment it is issued [[session.ttl]], and can be ended immediately by deleting it server-side [[session.revocable]] — which is the whole reason the token is opaque rather than a JWT.

There are no refresh tokens [[auth.no-refresh]]. A user whose session expires signs in again [[auth.reauth-on-expiry]].

sections.title: What the services behind it assume
sections.narrative:
The BFF forwards the verified user id inward on the `x-user-id` header [[session.forwarded-identity]]. Every domain API authorises on that header alone and performs no verification of its own [[api.trusts-header]].

> This is the load-bearing assumption of the whole design: **the header is trusted because the network is**. A domain API reachable by any route other than the BFF has no authentication at all. If that ever stops being true — a new ingress, a debugging port, a service mesh change — this document is wrong and the system is open.

sections.title: The two things that bypass it
sections.narrative:
Two paths do not carry a session.

Stripe calls the webhook endpoint directly and authenticates by signature instead [[webhook.signature]]. That endpoint is the one place a request from outside reaches a domain concern without passing a session check, and the signature is the only thing standing in its place.

The second is internal traffic between domain APIs, which is covered below rather than here: nothing currently documents how, or whether, those calls are authenticated.

sections.title: What this document does not cover
sections.narrative: Read this before trusting an absence. Something missing here is either out of scope below, listed as noticed-and-unaccounted-for, or nobody has looked.

glossary.definition: A session identifier that carries no information of its own: the server holds everything it means, so revoking it is a delete rather than a wait.

out_of_scope.area: How a user proves who they are in the first place
out_of_scope.reason: Sign-in, password handling and any identity provider are not documented here. This document starts at the point a session exists.
This covers who the caller is, not what they are allowed to do. Role and permission checks are not documented anywhere yet.

out_of_scope.area: Service-to-service calls inside the private network
out_of_scope.reason: Not documented yet. Whether the domain APIs authenticate each other is unknown, and the trust-the-header design means it matters.
Ops staff reach the Admin console, which uses the same BFF sessions, but no claim here covers how ops accounts differ from customer accounts.
